subject: 7A3285F9D060E1FFC9B67CEF57102DA7
introduction: In 1848, at Badasht, the Bábí poet Ṭáhirih appeared before a company of men without her veil; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá called the rigid veiling of Persian women “unspeakable” and said it shut them out of education. Yet when Bahá’í women in the East asked whether they should unveil he told them to wait, since dress must suit each country and a premature act would bring persecution on everyone. The guide gathers both kinds of statement. Paul’s rules about giving no offence and being “all things to all men” are the same prudence; his “vail upon their heart” is the veil that matters; Wollstonecraft and Mill say what the outward veil cost. The Qur’an’s own verse begins by telling men to lower their gaze.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá condemned the veil and counselled patience about removing it. Is that consistent?
When should a just change wait for a society to be ready, and who pays for the waiting?
What are the inward veils reading 2 has in mind?

outside.why: Qurratu’l-‘Ayn tore off her veils. When it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away.
Sometimes the veil is external and sometimes within. Now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.
Arise with a firm heart and an eloquent tongue. Deborah, a prophetess, judged Israel at that time.
The veil prevents education. Wollstonecraft: strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience.
Ṭáhirih, daughter of a priest. Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.
Covering must be according to what suits each country. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
Paul on adapting his own conduct to each people he lived among: I am made all things to all men.

Kindness to a sister uneasy about the veil. Peter moved adornment inward: not that outward adorning, but the hidden man of the heart. Does the readings’ advice about dress rest on principle, or on what a society can bear?
Women advised to wait. If meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth.

“In this Dispensation the veil is stricter than before”: a puzzling remark beside reading 1. The Qur’an’s rule begins with the men: tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest. What might be the veil that is stricter now?
Women yet to sit in the House of Representatives. Mill: the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong in itself, and one of the chief hindrances to human improvement.
